claim: Self-replicating gene drives that modify sex ratios or infer a fitness cost could be used to control populations of invasive alien species.
source: Self-replicating gene drives that modify sex ratios or infer a fitness cost could be used to control populations of invasive alien species.
evidence: This is a general statement about potential applications of gene drives, drawing on established scientific knowledge about gene drive technology.

claim: The targeted deletion of Y sex chromosomes using CRISPR technology offers a new approach for sex bias that could be incorporated within gene-drive designs.
source: The targeted deletion of Y sex chromosomes using CRISPR technology offers a new approach for sex bias that could be incorporated within gene-drive designs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental work and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas12a system can eliminate the Y chromosome in embryonic stem cells with high efficiency (c. 90%).
source: Firstly, we demonstrate that the CRISPR/Cas12a system can eliminate the Y chromosome in embryonic stem cells with high efficiency (c. 90%).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 showing qPCR results.

claim: A Y-shredding drive that progressively depletes the pool of XY males could effect population eradication through mate limitation.
source: Next, using stochastic, individual-based models of a pest mouse population, we show that a Y-shredding drive that progressively depletes the pool of XY males could effect population eradication through mate limitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3-7.

claim: A Y-CHOPE gene drive could be a viable tool for vertebrate pest control.
source: Our molecular and modeling data suggest that a Y-CHOPE gene drive could be a viable tool for vertebrate pest control.
evidence: This conclusion is based on both the experimental Y-shredding efficiency data and the modeling results showing population eradication.

claim: The engineering of 'selfish' gene drives, with biased inheritance, has become increasingly feasible since the advent of the CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing system.
source: The engineering of 'selfish' gene drives, with biased inheritance (Burt, 2003), has become increasingly feasible since the advent of the CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing system (Esvelt et al., 2014; Gantz and Bier, 2015; Champer et al., 2016; Galizi et al., 2016; Hammond et al., 2016; Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on CRISPR-based gene drives.

claim: Gene drive technology could be used to address a range of environmental problems, including the control of invasive (or overabundant) sexually reproducing animal populations.
source: By spreading genetic elements through the genomes of wild populations, this technology could be used to address a range of environmental problems, including the control of invasive (or overabundant) sexually reproducing animal populations (Prowse et al., 2017; McFarlane et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work discussing applications of gene drives.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 gene drives are single-copy transgenic elements that encode the Cas9 endonuclease and a site-specific guide RNA (gRNA) that together act to cleave a matching target site on the homologous chromosome.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 gene drives are single-copy transgenic elements that encode the Cas9 endonuclease and a site-specific guide RNA (gRNA) that together act to cleave a matching target site on the homologous chromosome.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism of CRISPR/Cas9 gene drives based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Repair of the DNA break via homologous recombination (HR) results in replication (or 'homing') of the gene-drive construct.
source: Repair of the DNA break via homologous recombination (HR) results in replication (or 'homing') of the gene-drive construct (Burt, 2003; Sinkins and Gould, 2006).
evidence: This claim describes the homing mechanism and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: If the homing mechanism is triggered in the germline, recessive traits that negatively impact the fitness of homozygous individuals should still spread though populations, and eventually lead to population suppression or eradication.
source: If the homing mechanism is triggered in the germline (Bruck, 1957; Burt, 2003), recessive traits that negatively impact the fitness of homozygous individuals should still spread though populations, and eventually lead to population suppression or eradication (Deredec et al., 2008; Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work on gene drives.

claim: Invasive alien species (IAS) threaten the conservation of biological diversity.
source: Invasive alien species (IAS) threaten the conservation of biological diversity (Bellard et al., 2016; Early et al., 2016), impact human health (Mazza et al., 2014), and have severe economic consequences around the globe (Pimentel et al., 2005; Hoffmann and Broadhurst, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on the impacts of invasive species.

claim: Invasive alien species impact human health.
source: Invasive alien species (IAS) threaten the conservation of biological diversity (Bellard et al., 2016; Early et al., 2016), impact human health (Mazza et al., 2014), and have severe economic consequences around the globe (Pimentel et al., 2005; Hoffmann and Broadhurst, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on health impacts of invasive species.

claim: Invasive alien species have severe economic consequences around the globe.
source: Invasive alien species (IAS) threaten the conservation of biological diversity (Bellard et al., 2016; Early et al., 2016), impact human health (Mazza et al., 2014), and have severe economic consequences around the globe (Pimentel et al., 2005; Hoffmann and Broadhurst, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on economic impacts of invasive species.

claim: The human-mediated transport of vertebrate pests has contributed substantially to species' extinctions.
source: In particular, the human-mediated transport of vertebrate pests has contributed substantially to species' extinctions (Woinarski et al., 2015; Spatz et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2018) and loss of agricultural production (Gong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on species extinctions caused by vertebrate pests.

claim: The human-mediated transport of vertebrate pests has contributed substantially to loss of agricultural production.
source: In particular, the human-mediated transport of vertebrate pests has contributed substantially to species' extinctions (Woinarski et al., 2015; Spatz et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2018) and loss of agricultural production (Gong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on agricultural impacts of vertebrate pests.

claim: There is considerable interest in the potential of gene-drive technology as a novel tool for controlling vertebrate pest populations.
source: Consequently, there is considerable interest in the potential of gene-drive technology as a novel tool for controlling vertebrate pest populations (Johnson et al., 2016; Prowse et al., 2017; Moro et al., 2018), which could be used in combination with traditional control methods.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work discussing gene drives for vertebrate pest control.

claim: Gene-drive technology could be used in combination with traditional control methods.
source: Consequently, there is considerable interest in the potential of gene-drive technology as a novel tool for controlling vertebrate pest populations (Johnson et al., 2016; Prowse et al., 2017; Moro et al., 2018), which could be used in combination with traditional control methods.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of gene drives.

claim: Rodent pests have considerable negative impacts on island biodiversity.
source: Given the considerable negative impacts of rodent pests on island biodiversity (Spatz et al., 2017), and the risks associated with the unintended dispersal of gene-drive carriers beyond target populations (Webber et al., 2015), the eradication of invasive rodent populations on islands is a powerful model system for testing the efficacy of gene-drive technology (Prowse et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on rodent impacts on islands.

claim: There are risks associated with the unintended dispersal of gene-drive carriers beyond target populations.
source: Given the considerable negative impacts of rodent pests on island biodiversity (Spatz et al., 2017), and the risks associated with the unintended dispersal of gene-drive carriers beyond target populations (Webber et al., 2015), the eradication of invasive rodent populations on islands is a powerful model system for testing the efficacy of gene-drive technology (Prowse et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on gene drive risks.

claim: The eradication of invasive rodent populations on islands is a powerful model system for testing the efficacy of gene-drive technology.
source: Given the considerable negative impacts of rodent pests on island biodiversity (Spatz et al., 2017), and the risks associated with the unintended dispersal of gene-drive carriers beyond target populations (Webber et al., 2015), the eradication of invasive rodent populations on islands is a powerful model system for testing the efficacy of gene-drive technology (Prowse et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about suitable model systems.

claim: Gene drives for population control could be designed to spread a recessive mutation that causes infertility or lethality.
source: At their simplest, gene drives for population control could be designed to spread a recessive mutation that causes infertility or lethality (Burt, 2003; Deredec et al., 2008; Gantz et al., 2015; Hammond et al., 2016; Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work on gene drives.

claim: The gene-drive cassette can be positioned within the genome to inactivate a haplosufficient gene required for fertility or embryonic development.
source: To achieve this, the gene-drive cassette is positioned within the genome to inactivate a haplosufficient gene required for fertility or embryonic development.
evidence: This describes a strategy for gene drive design based on established knowledge.

claim: Assuming homing occurs in the germline, heterozygotes are unaffected and spread the drive through sexual reproduction, whereas the sterility or embryonic non-viability of homozygotes results in population suppression.
source: Assuming homing occurs in the germline, heterozygotes are unaffected and spread the drive through sexual reproduction, whereas the sterility or embryonic non-viability of homozygotes results in population suppression.
evidence: This is an inference about how gene drives would function based on genetic principles.

claim: In silico modeling has confirmed that gene drives targeting fertility or viability could be viable for a number of insect species.
source: In silico modeling has confirmed this approach could be viable for a number of insect species (Burt, 2003; Deredec et al., 2008; Unckless et al., 2015), and also small populations of invasive vertebrates (i.e. mice, rats and rabbits) on islands (Prowse et al., 2017; Wilkins et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: In silico modeling has confirmed that gene drives targeting fertility or viability could be viable for small populations of invasive vertebrates (i.e. mice, rats and rabbits) on islands.
source: In silico modeling has confirmed this approach could be viable for a number of insect species (Burt, 2003; Deredec et al., 2008; Unckless et al., 2015), and also small populations of invasive vertebrates (i.e. mice, rats and rabbits) on islands (Prowse et al., 2017; Wilkins et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: An alternative strategy is to design a gene drive that achieves population suppression by biasing offspring sex ratios so that one sex become limiting.
source: An alternative strategy is to design a gene drive that achieves population suppression by biasing offspring sex ratios so that one sex become limiting (Windbichler et al., 2008; Galizi et al., 2014; Galizi et al., 2016; Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on sex-ratio distorting gene drives.

claim: One approach to sex-ratio distortion is to introduce genetic 'cargo' which, when expressed, causes a phenotypic change during offspring development.
source: One approach to sex-ratio distortion is to introduce genetic 'cargo' which, when expressed, causes a phenotypic change during offspring development.
evidence: This describes a general strategy for sex-ratio distortion based on established knowledge.

claim: In mice, presence of the Y-linked Sry gene causes XX females to develop as sterile males.
source: In mice, for example, presence of the Y-linked Sry gene causes XX females to develop as sterile males (Koopman et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on sex determination in mice.

claim: Biased inheritance of an autosomally integrated Sry construct could be achieved by linkage to a naturally occurring selfish element (the t-haplotype) or a synthetic gene-drive.
source: Biased inheritance of an autosomally integrated Sry construct could be achieved by linkage to a naturally occurring selfish element (the t-haplotype; Campbell et al., 2015) or a synthetic gene-drive (Prowse et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on selfish genetic elements and gene drives.

claim: Since sterile heterozygous females cannot spread the construct, population suppression using an Sry-based strategy requires the regular release of gene-drive carriers.
source: Since sterile heterozygous females cannot spread the construct, however, population suppression using this strategy requires the regular release of gene-drive carriers (Backus and Gross, 2016; Prowse et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of Sry-based strategies, supported by citations.

claim: Incorporating spermatogenesis genes to convert females into fertile males could potentially overcome the drawback of requiring regular releases.
source: This drawback could potentially be overcome by incorporating the spermatogenesis genes required to convert females into fertile males; modeling indicates such a drive could achieve population eradication by reducing the availability of female breeding stock, but its spread would rely upon normal spermatogenesis in sex-reversed XX males (Prowse et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Kyrou et al. (2018) demonstrated a CRISPR-based gene drive targeting the female version of the gene doublesex in the mosquito Anopheles gambiae.
source: Notably, Kyrou et al. (2018) recently demonstrated a simpler sex-distorting approach by engineering a CRISPR-based gene drive targeting the female version of the gene doublesex in the mosquito Anopheles gambiae.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: When introduced to caged mosquito populations at a frequency of 12.5%, the doublesex-targeting drive spread rapidly, converting homozygous females into sterile individuals with an intersex phenotype, and leading to total population collapse.
source: When introduced to caged mosquito populations at a frequency of 12.5%, the drive spread rapidly, converting homozygous females into sterile individuals with an intersex phenotype, and leading to total population collapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work by Kyrou et al. (2018).

claim: The targeted deletion of allosomes (X or Y sex chromosomes) offers another approach to sex reversal that could potentially be incorporated within gene-drive designs.
source: The targeted deletion of allosomes (X or Y sex chromosomes) offers another approach to sex reversal that could potentially be incorporated within gene-drive designs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of chromosome deletion technology.

claim: In many species the abundance of mature females is a primary determinant of the population growth rate.
source: To date, most research has focused on male-biasing X-shredding strategies, because in many species the abundance of mature females is a primary determinant of the population growth rate.
evidence: This is based on established ecological knowledge about population dynamics.

claim: In Anopheles gambiae, a single-copy autosomal integration of the endonuclease I-PpoI was sufficient to shred the paternal X chromosome during meiosis, resulting in fertile males that produced >95% male offspring.
source: In Anopheles gambiae, for example, a single-copy autosomal integration of the endonuclease I-PpoI was sufficient to shred the paternal X chromosome during meiosis, resulting in fertile males that produced >95% male offspring (Galizi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The I-PpoI X-shredding approach effectively suppressed small caged populations of mosquitoes under a multiple-release strategy.
source: This approach effectively suppressed small caged populations of mosquitoes under a multiple-release strategy (Galizi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: In Anopheles gambiae, a CRISPR-Cas9 system targeting an X-linked rDNA sequence achieved a male bias of between 86% and 95%.
source: In the same species, a CRISPR-Cas9 system targeting an X-linked rDNA sequence achieved a male bias of between 86% and 95% (Galizi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: X-shredding DNA cassettes could be spread by integration within the Y chromosome if X-shredding activity could be limited to the meiotic period.
source: X-shredding DNA cassettes could be spread by integration within the Y chromosome if X-shredding activity could be limited to the meiotic period (i.e. the Y-drive; Hamilton, 1967, Deredec et al., 2011, Galizi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Elimination of the murine Y chromosome in cultured cells and embryos has been achieved using a CRISPR/Cas9 system adapted from Streptococcus pyogenes (Sp) incorporating gRNA(s) that target multiple chromosomal locations simultaneously.
source: Recently, elimination of the murine Y chromosome in cultured cells and embryos has been achieved using a CRISPR/Cas9 system adapted from Streptococcus pyogenes (Sp) incorporating gRNA(s) that target multiple chromosomal locations simultaneously (Adikusuma et al., 2017; Zuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The efficiency of Y chromosome shredding using CRISPR/Cas9 was high (up to 80%) and did not appear to negatively impact cell or embryo viability.
source: The efficiency of Y chromosome shredding was high (up to 80%) and did not appear to negatively impact cell or embryo viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work by Adikusuma et al. (2017) and Zuo et al. (2017).

claim: Y-chromosome deletion in mice converts XY males into XO females, which are not only viable but are also known to be fertile in the laboratory and in the wild.
source: Y-chromosome deletion in mice converts XY males into XO females, which are not only viable but are also known to be fertile in the laboratory (Kaufman, 1972; Probst et al., 2008) and in the wild (Searle and Jones, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on XO mice.

claim: The spread of a Y-shredding drive would bias offspring sex ratios towards females through the production of XX- and XO-genotype offspring.
source: The spread of a Y-shredding drive would bias offspring sex ratios towards females through the production of XX- and XO-genotype offspring, and population control should be achieved once males become limiting (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference about how the Y-CHOPE drive would function, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Population control using a Y-shredding drive should be achieved once males become limiting.
source: The spread of a Y-shredding drive would bias offspring sex ratios towards females through the production of XX- and XO-genotype offspring, and population control should be achieved once males become limiting (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of population control, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A Y-CHOPE strategy would require two different CRISPR endonucleases because the homing and the Y-shredding processes occur at different times and target different sequences.
source: Since the homing and the Y-shredding processes occur at different times and target different sequences, a Y-CHOPE strategy would require two different CRISPR endonucleases.
evidence: This is an inference about the technical requirements of the Y-CHOPE strategy.

claim: To date, only one programmable endonuclease (SpCas9) has been used for gene-drive homing and Y-shredding.
source: However, to date, only one programmable endonuclease (SpCas9) has been used for gene-drive homing and Y-shredding.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field based on knowledge of prior work.

claim: The gRNA Centro 37X-A eliminated nearly 90% of the Y-chromosomes in the cell population based on qPCR analyses of sequences at the termini of short and long arms.
source: In particular, the gRNA Centro 37X-A eliminated nearly 90% of the Y-chromosomes in the cell population based on qPCR analyses of sequences at the termini of short and long arms (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The efficiency of Centro 37X-A is slightly higher than previously published Y chromosome deletion experiments using SpCas9 (~80% efficiency).
source: This efficiency is slightly higher than our previously published Y chromosome deletion experiments using SpCas9 (~80% efficiency; Adikusuma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim compares current results to prior published work.

claim: All three Cas12a gRNAs targeting the Y long arm showed shredding activity, although none exceeded the efficiency of gRNA Centro 37X-A.
source: All these gRNAs showed shredding activity, although none exceeded the efficiency of gRNA Centro 37X-A (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Centromere shredding using Cas12a provides an efficient approach for Y-chromosome deletion.
source: We therefore conclude that centromere shredding using Cas12a provides an efficient approach for Y-chromosome deletion.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Individual-based simulations demonstrate that a Y-chromosome shredding gene drive strategy is capable of eradicating a pest vertebrate population.
source: Individual-based simulations of the Y-chromosome shredding gene drive demonstrate that this strategy is capable of eradicating a pest vertebrate population (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Using baseline parameterization, eradication of a population of 10,000 mice was guaranteed when assuming perfect Y-shredding efficiency and 100% homologous recombination.
source: Using our baseline parameterization, eradication of a population of 10,000 mice was guaranteed when we assumed a perfect Y-shredding efficiency and 100% homologous recombination following Cas9 activity so that resistant alleles could not evolve (Figure 3a(i)).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3a(i).

claim: Under perfect conditions, the gene drive spread rapidly through the population, converting XY males to XO females until males became limiting and the population began to decline.
source: Under these conditions, the gene drive spread rapidly through the population, converting XY males to XO females until males became limiting and the population began to decline (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observed population trajectories changed as a function of the mating system simulated.
source: However, the observed population trajectories changed as a function of the mating system simulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results comparing different mating systems in Figure 3.

claim: Assuming short-term monogamy (Fmax = 1), male limitation occurred rapidly and the population size declined smoothly from carrying capacity to extinction.
source: Assuming short-term monogamy (Fmax = 1), male limitation occurred rapidly and the population size declined smoothly from carrying capacity to extinction (Figure 2b(i)).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 2b(i) (likely referring to Figure 3b(i)).

claim: As higher levels of polygyny were simulated, the sex-biasing effect of the drive increased the reproductive potential of the population initially, causing a short period of population growth.
source: In contrast, as higher levels of polygyny were simulated by increasing the maximum number of mates allowed per male, the sex-biasing effect of the drive increased the reproductive potential of the population initially (Figure 2c(i)). This caused a short period of population growth, until the proportion of females breeding was reduced due to male limitation, after which populations declined to extinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 2c(i) (likely referring to Figure 3c(i)).

claim: The simulated probability of eradication decreased as the Y-shredding efficiency was reduced.
source: The simulated probability of eradication decreased as the Y-shredding efficiency was reduced, but there was a clear interaction with the level of polygyny assumed.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a clear interaction between Y-shredding efficiency and the level of polygyny assumed in determining eradication probability.
source: The simulated probability of eradication decreased as the Y-shredding efficiency was reduced, but there was a clear interaction with the level of polygyny assumed.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Assuming PY = 0.75, extinction was still guaranteed for a population exhibiting short-term monogamy.
source: Assuming PY = 0.75, for example, extinction was still guaranteed for a population exhibiting short-term monogamy (Figure 3a(ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3a(ii).

claim: Under polygyny breeding (Fmax = 3) with PY = 0.75, introduction of the gene drive produced population growth followed by suppression to a new stable state below carrying capacity.
source: Under polygyny breeding (Fmax = 3), however, introduction of the gene drive produced population growth followed by suppression to a new stable state below carrying capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: When PY was reduced to 0.5, permanent population suppression (but not eradication) typically resulted under short-term monogamous mating.
source: When PY was reduced still further to 0.5, permanent population suppression (but not eradication) typically resulted under short-term monogamous mating (Figure 3b(iii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3b(iii).

claim: With PY = 0.5 under polygynous breeding, population growth to a new carrying capacity (above the initial carrying capacity) was observed because the sex-ratio bias toward females increased reproductive potential without causing male limitation.
source: However, population growth to a new carrying capacity (above the initial carrying capacity) was observed under polygynous breeding because the sex-ratio bias toward females increased reproductive potential without causing male limitation (Figure 3c(iii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3c(iii).

claim: The failure of simulated eradication under low Y-shredding efficiencies was not due to a lack of spread.
source: In these cases, the failure of the simulated eradication attempt under low Y-shredding efficiencies was not due to a lack of spread.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The drive spread rapidly to fixation when non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) was precluded (PN = 0.1), but the sex-ratio distortion produced was insufficient to cause males to become limiting.
source: In fact, the drive spread rapidly to fixation when non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) was precluded (PN = 0.1), but the sex-ratio distortion produced was insufficient to cause males to become limiting (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Placement of the gene drive within a non-coding region failed to produce simulated eradications when DNA mutations produced due to NHEJ was modeled (PN = 0.1), even when perfect Y-shredding efficiency was assumed.
source: Placement of the gene drive within a non-coding region failed to produce simulated eradications when DNA mutations produced due to NHEJ was modeled (PN = 0.1), even when perfect Y-shredding efficiency was assumed (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Under non-coding placement with NHEJ, the initial spread of the gene was reversed following the evolution of resistant alleles that could never acquire the drive.
source: Under these conditions, the initial spread of the gene was reversed following the evolution of resistant alleles that could never acquire the drive.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Gene-drive-positive alleles were purged from the population due to selection against sub-fertile XO females when resistant alleles evolved.
source: In such cases, gene-drive-positive alleles were purged from the population due to selection against sub-fertile XO females.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of gene drive failure based on modeling results.

claim: Using a gene-drive design with placement in a haploinsufficient gene, population eradication could be achieved with a high PN of 0.1.
source: Using this gene-drive design, population eradication could be achieved with a high PN of 0.1 (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: The Y-shredding efficiency required to guarantee extinction increased with the level of polygyny assumed for mice.
source: The Y-shredding efficiency required to guarantee extinction increased with the level of polygyny assumed for mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Assuming short-term monogamy, Y-shredding efficiencies exceeding 0.67 could guarantee extinction.
source: Assuming short-term monogamy, for example, Y-shredding efficiencies exceeding 0.67 could guarantee extinction (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Allowing up to 3 and 5 mates per male increases the Y-shredding efficiency required for certain eradication to 0.87 and 0.92, respectively.
source: In contrast, allowing up to 3 and 5 mates per male increases the Y-shredding efficiency required for certain eradication to 0.87 and 0.92, respectively (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The Y-linked X-shredding drive is not influenced by polygyny, because females become the limiting sex.
source: The Y-linked X-shredding drive is not influenced by polygyny, because females become the limiting sex.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of X-shredding drives based on biological principles.

claim: The suppression achieved by an X-shredding strategy could be inferior to a Y-shredder when the breeding system of the target species approached short-term monogamy or when the probability of inheriting a Y chromosome from a germline YO male was similar to Mendelian rates.
source: However, our comparative simulations indicated that the suppression achieved by this strategy could be inferior to a Y-shredder when: (1) the breeding system of the target species approached short-term monogamy or (2) the probability of inheriting a Y chromosome from a germline YO male was similar to Mendelian rates (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative modeling results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Global sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the mating system of the target species (Fmax) and the Y-shredding efficiency (PY) were the primary determinants of simulation outcomes, with relative-influence scores from the boosted regression tree BRT emulator of 29% and 28%, respectively.
source: Global sensitivity analysis for the Y-CHOPE strategy, using Latin hypercube sampling of the parameter space, demonstrated that the mating system of the target species (Fmax) and the Y-shredding efficiency (PY) were the primary determinants of simulation outcomes, with relative-influence scores from the boosted regression tree BRT emulator of 29% and 28%, respectively (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The number of homing gRNAs, which strongly influenced the probability that homing occurred successfully, was also influential in determining simulation outcomes.
source: The number of homing gRNAs, which strongly influenced the probability that homing occurred successfully, was also influential (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Assumptions regarding the sub-fertility of XO females had less influence on simulation results.
source: Assumptions regarding the sub-fertility of XO females had less influence on simulation results.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The placement of the Y-shredding drive within a haploinsufficient gene is robust to PN up to 0.1, at least for a starting population size of 10,000 mice.
source: Partial dependency plots illustrated that the placement of the Y-shredding drive within a haploinsufficient gene robust to PN up to 0.1, at least for a starting population size of 10,000 mice, but higher probabilities of NHEJ produced low probabilities of eradication (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Higher probabilities of NHEJ (>0.1) produced low probabilities of eradication.
source: Partial dependency plots illustrated that the placement of the Y-shredding drive within a haploinsufficient gene robust to PN up to 0.1, at least for a starting population size of 10,000 mice, but higher probabilities of NHEJ produced low probabilities of eradication (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 7b.

claim: When single-site mutations arising through NHEJ were not assumed to guarantee non-functionality of the developmental gene (i.e. Pnf <1), probabilities of eradication peaked when the Y-shredding efficiency was also less than 1.
source: Interestingly, when single-site mutations arising through NHEJ were not assumed to guarantee non-functionality of the developmental gene (i.e. Pnf <1), probabilities of eradication peaked when the Y-shredding efficiency was also less than 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The successful eradication of vertebrate pests on islands has been greatly aided by the adoption of new combinatorial technologies.
source: The successful eradication of vertebrate pests on islands has been greatly aided by the adoption of new combinatorial technologies (Howald et al., 2007; Gregory et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on pest eradication.

claim: New innovative tools are required to complement existing approaches and extend eradication efforts to increasingly large target populations.

claim: 100,000 parameter samples were sufficient to generate robust sensitivity metrics, as confirmed by asymptotic behavior of the emulator performance and sensitivity measures.
source: To confirm that 100,000 parameter samples were sufficient to generate robust sensitivity metrics, we used the approach recommended by Prowse et al. (2016). In brief, we emulated the sensitivity-analysis output for parameter subsamples of increasing size (i.e. between 1000 and the complete 100,000 samples). We then confirmed that the cross-validatory performance of the emulator and the sensitivity measures derived from it exhibited asymptotic behavior (relative influence metrics for the 10 parameters converged well before 100,000 samples; see Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.
